The following general strategies are derived from those suggested in the text on page 69.  Some commentary has also been added.  These strategies are often, but not invariably, helpful.  They are given in the order in which they should be applied, i.e. first consider whether Strategy 1 is applicable, then whether Strategy 2 is applicable, and so forth.  Note that as a result of applying one of the latter strategies, an earlier strategy, previously inapplicable, may become applicable.`$`-Most derivations begin with a show line containing the conclusion of the argument.`$1`+`=

If the conditions for boxing and canceling occur, do it.`$2`+If the WFF in the last uncanceled show line occurs unboxed, below the show line, box and cancel by Direct Derivation (DD).  Don't forget to cite the line number.`$A`-`=

If the WFF in the last uncanceled show line is a conditional, and its consequent occurs unboxed, below the show line, box and cancel by Conditional Derivation (CD).  Don't forget to cite the line number.`$B`-`=
If a WFF and the negation of that WFF occur on separate unboxed lines, below the last uncanceled show line, box and cancel by Indirect Derivation (ID).  Don't forget to cite both line numbers.`$C`-`=
If a WFF that is needed for boxing and canceling occurs in an antecedent line above the last uncanceled show line, use Repetition (R) to bring it below the show line.`$3`+`=

To derive a conditional, use conditional derivation.`$4`+If the last uncanceled show line is a conditional, follow it immediately by a line in which you assume the antecedent of the conditional (unless the antecedent of the conditional already occurs in earlier, unboxed line).  The assumption line would be justified, "ASS CD".`$A`-`=
If you have already obtained the antecedent, enter a show line in which you attempt to show the consequent (unless the consequent already occurs in an antecedent line).`$B`-`=

To derive a conjunction, derive first both conjuncts, and then use Adjunction (ADJ).`$5`+If the last uncanceled show line is a conjunction, enter a show line in which you attempt to show the first conjunct (unless the first conjunct already occurs in an antecedent line).`$A`-`=
If you have already obtained the first conjunct, attempt to show the second conjunct (unless it already occurs in an antecedent line).`$B`-`=
When you have obtained the two conjuncts in separate lines, apply the rule of Adjunction (ADJ) to the two lines in order to derive the conjunction.`$C`-`=
You can then box and cancel the original show line by Direct Derivation (DD).`$D`-`=

To derive a biconditional, derive first the two corresponding conditionals, and then use Conditional-Biconditional (CB).`$6`+If the last uncanceled show line is a biconditional, enter a show line in which you attempt to show the first (left to right) of the corresponding conditionals (unless the first of the corresponding conditionals already occurs in an antecedent line).`$A`-`=
If you have obtained the first conditional, attempt to show the second conditional (unless it already occurs in an antecedent line).`$B`-`=
When you have obtained the two conditionals in separate lines, apply the rule of Conditional-Biconditional (CB) to the two lines in order to derive the biconditional.`$C`-`=
You can then box and cancel the original show line by Direct Derivation (DD).`$D`-`=

To derive a disjunction, derive first the corresponding conditional, and then use Conditional Disjunction (CDJ).`$7`+If the last uncanceled show line has the form \l(P | Q)\l, enter a show line in which you attempt to show the corresponding conditional: \l(~P -> Q)\l (unless it already occurs in an antecedent line).  Conditionals are relatively easy to show by using Strategic Hint 3 (above).`$A`-`=

If you have obtained the conditional, apply the rule Conditional Disjunction (CDJ), which has the form: \l(~P -> Q) .: (P | Q)\l.  You will thereby derive the original disjunction in the show line.`$B`-`=
If CDJ is not an available rule, you can either use T45, BC, and MP, or, if T45 is not available, you can mimic the argument given in the text (p. 76) for the second half of T45.`$C`-`=
You can then box and cancel the original show line by Direct Derivation (DD).`$D`-`=

To derive anything else, use indirect derivation unless another procedure is immediately obvious.`$9`+If the last uncanceled show line is a negation or a sentence letter (or, in Chapter III, an existential or universal generalization), follow it immediately by a line in which you assume the negation of the show line (unless the negation of the show line already occurs in an antecedent line).  The assumption line would be justified, "ASS ID".`$A`-`=
It is generally valuable to enter some assumption line immediately following a show line because it gives you more lines to work with.`$B`-`=

Whenever a sentence follows from antecedent lines by MP, MT, S, MTP, or BC, enter that sentence as a line.`$10`+Whenever a conditional that has not yet been used occurs in an antecedent line, apply Modus Ponens (MP) or Modus Tollens (MT) if possible.`$A`-`=
Whenever a disjunction that has not yet been used occurs in an antecedent line, apply Modus Tollendo Ponens (MTP) if possible.`$B`-`=
Whenever a conjunction occurs in an antecedent line, apply Simplification (S) to obtain any conjunct not already available.`$C`-`=
Whenever a biconditional occurs in an antecedent line, apply Biconditional-Conditional (BC) to obtain any conditional not already available.`$D`-`=
You may generate some unnecessary lines in this way, but it gives you more to work with.`$E`-`=

If a conditional occurs in an antecedent line, and has not yet been used, it is often helpful to attempt to show its antecedent (or, alternatively, the negation of its consequent).`$11`+If successful, this would allow you to apply MP (or, MT).`$A`-`=

If a disjunction occurs in an antecedent line, and has not yet been used, it is often helpful to attempt to show the negation of one of its disjuncts).`$12`+If successful, this would allow you to apply MTP.`$A`-`=

When using indirect derivation, determine whether any of the antecedent lines is the negation of a conditional (conjunction, disjunction, or biconditional); if so, attempt to derive that conditional (conjunction, disjunction, or biconditional).`$13`+Conditionals are usually easiest to derive, but if an antecedent line is the negation of a conjunction, disjunction, or biconditional, it is often useful to attempt to derive that conjunction, disjunction, or biconditional.`$A`-`=

"When using indirect derivation" simply means that at some earlier stage, an uncompleted indirect derivation was begun.  If so, there will be an (unboxed) antecedent line justified by "ASS ID".`$B`-`=
Whenever Double Negation (DN) would help provide the conditions for 2, 3, 10-13, apply it.`$14`+`=

When using indirect derivation, and none of the above Strategic Hints is applicable, it is sometimes useful to begin attempting to derive the individual sentence letters (or their negations) that appear in antecedent lines.`$15`+Entering "Show P", allows one to assume "~P"; entering "Show ~Q", allows one to assume "Q".  Eventually, the buildup of these lines may allow you to apply Strategic Hints 8 - 11.  If you are successful in boxing and cancelling such lines as "Show P" and "Show ~Q", you will have to repeat the use of Hints 6 and 7 to complete the derivation.`$A`-`=

01`sDerInf001`nuniform derivation`iWhen a Show line is canceled, the program notes whether it was by a "Uniform Derivation" (one in which the assumption matches the basis for boxing and canceling) or by a "Mixed Derivation" (one in which they do not).  No error is involved in either case, but the program calls it to your attention.  \n\nThis message is for information only.  Info messages appear against the usual blue background.  Error messages appear against a red background.`x

02`sDerInf002`nmixed derivation`iWhen a Show line is canceled, the program notes whether it was by a "Uniform Derivation" (one in which the assumption matches the basis for boxing and canceling) or by a "Mixed Derivation" (one in which they do not).  No error is involved in either case, but the program calls it to your attention.  \n\nThis message is for information only.  Info messages appear against the usual blue background.  Error messages appear against a red background.`x

03`sDerInf003`nblank line`iIt is not strictly incorrect to include a blank line, but the program calls it to your attention.  A line can be deleted either by using the Alt+Delete key combination or by using the Toolbox that appears by right-clicking the mouse.  \n\nThis message is for information only.  Info messages appear against the usual blue background.  Error messages appear against a red background.`x

04`sDerInf004`nnothing to check`iThe WFF field is blank.

This message is generated by a Check, and will appear even if the Justification field contains a putative justification.  

If there is something in the Justification field, and Command Mode is enabled, you may regard the justification as a command, and attempt to execute it by placing the cursor in the Justification field, and pressing Shift+Enter.  The command will then be executed, or, if there is an error in the justification, a different message will appear.`xThis INFO message is generated by a Check.  Note that this message will appear even if there is a justification, including a fallacious justification that would generate a different error message in Command Mode (e.g. when referencing a line with a parse error).`d

07`sDerErrTxt`n<text>`eThis explanation is intended to serve for many different messages.

Messages of the form "can not map xxx to yyy" indicate that the substitution you proposed in answer to a query was of the wrong grammatical type.  For example, if you answered a query for an instantial term with "P", such a message would be generated because "P" is a sentence letter and not a term.  Similarly, if you were introducing an instance of a theorem, and answered a query for a substitution instance of "Q" with "x", the message "can not map Q to x" would be generated because "x" is a variable, and cannot replace a sentence letter.

Messages of the form "parse error at token n" indicate that the expression in the WFF field is not well-formed.  The parser believes that the first error occurs at about the nth symbol.

Messages of the form "lexical error at token n" indicate that the expression in the WFF field contains a symbol that is not in the vocabulary of the language.  The parser believes that the first such occurs at about the nth symbol.`xI added this for some auto-generated messages that should probably have entries elsewhere in this database.`d

<indent 5>ASS CD 
(the assumption for conditional derivation), and 

<indent 5>ASS ID 
(the assumption for indirect derivation).`x

It is likely that the error was a failure to use a separator between a line reference and a rule name.  Almost any character other than a letter or a numeral will do as a separator.  Many people use a space or a comma.`xJUST field parser?`d

15`sDerErr008`n<rule name> must be on the last line of a subderivation`eYou appear to be attempting to Box and Cancel on a line that has other lines from the same subderivation below it. You may Box and Cancel only in the bottom line of a subderivation. This subderivation contains <branch lines left> below the present line.

You may wish to delete <branch lines left> or the present line using the Alt+Delete key combination. 

To recreate the present line at the bottom of the subderivation, add a new, empty line as follows: First verify that that the subderivation is not already boxed. If it is, Unbox using Ctrl+Shift+X. Then place the cursor in the present bottom line of the subderivation, and press Alt+Enter. (In Command Mode, Alt+Enter produces a new line without executing any command.)`x

07`sSymNot007`nYou create an Answer by working the problem and then clicking Add in
the Answer Manager. You can use the Direct entry button to quickly
create an answer, which will appear in the workspace (with empty text
boxes), from which you can use Answer/Add to add it to the list of
answers. You can add as many Answers as you wish, either right from
the workspace or starting out from the Direct entry facility.

To be added to the Answer list, every branch of the workspace answer
must terminate in an Atomic expression.

If you wish to edit one of the Answers in the list, perhaps to fill
in or change what is in the text boxes, click on the Answer to select
it, and click Enter to put it into the workspace. Edit it in the
workspace. When you are finished editing it, reopen the Answer
Manager, select the Answer and click Replace to replace the original
answer with the edited answer. You can also use Delete to remove any
Answer in the list.

Be sure to fill in the text boxes of your favorite answer(s) if you
wish the Hint facility to be able to offer fully explanatory hints.
If you wish to suppress Hints for certain Instructor Problems, use
only the 800 versions of those problem in your Assignments.

Only Problems with at least one Answer can be Uploaded.`xAnswer Manager help message`d

without parentheses as required by the syntax). On the right, enter

lines: #  problem:                 problem name, as shown in the problem list
#  options:                 per-problem options, e.g. eg (a worked example)
#  note:                    note shown under the problem title
#  common-name:             common name of the problem (course database)
#  original-name:           name the problem was copied from
#  seconds:                 time worked, in seconds (saved work)
#  notation:                chosen notation: O official, I informal, N not well formed
#  expansion:               which parse-tree nodes are expanded
#  problem:                 problem name, as shown in the problem list
#  options:                 per-problem options, e.g. eg (a worked example)
#  note:                    note shown under the problem title
#  common-name:             common name of the problem (course database)
#  original-name:           name the problem was copied from
#  seconds:                 time worked, in seconds (saved work)
#  correct-rules:           rules that are accepted as correct answers, separated by '.'
#  near-miss-rules:         rules that get a 'nearly right' response
#  comment:                 comment shown after a correct answer
#-The primitive rules of this chapter are:

Recog 1.001`$P->P . P  .: P`=This is a perfectly correct application of MP.  The fact that the rule is stated using distinct antecedent and consequent allows the antecedent and consequent to be distinct, but does not require it.`&
Recog 1.002`$~T->(T->U) . ~(T->U)  .: ~~T`=Note that the conclusion must be as given, and cannot be "T", which is not the negation of the antecedent of the conditional.`&
Recog 1.004`$~(~P->W)  .: P->W`=The premise is the negation of a conditional, not the negation of a negation.  If the premise had been \l"~~(P->W)"\l the conclusion could have been obtained by DN.`&

Recog 1.005`$~Q->~R . R  .: Q`=The second premise is not the negation of the consequent of the conditional (as is required), and the conclusion is not the negation of the antecedent of the conditional (as is also required).  The result can be obtained from those two premises, but not directly by a single application of MT.  Rather, one must first apply DN to the second premise, then apply MT to obtain \l"~~Q"\l, then apply a second DN to that result.`&
Recog 1.007`$(~Q->S)->P . ~Q->S  .: P`=Note that the "official" outermost parentheses have been dropped in the second premise, but cannot be dropped in the first premise.`&

Recog 1.009`$~~P->~Q . ~~Q  .: ~P`=This case is rather like 1.005.  Although MT can be applied directly to these premises, it yields \l"~~~P"\l rather than \l"~P"\l.  The latter requires an application of DN.`&
Recog 1.010`$T->S  .: ~~(T->S)`=As in 1.007, the "official" outermost parentheses have been dropped in the premise, but cannot be dropped in the conclusion.`&

Recog 1.011`$P->Y . ~P  .: ~Y`=A wrong way around attempt to apply MT.  To apply MT, the second premise must be the negation of the consequent of the conditional rather than being the negation of the antecedent.`&
Recog 1.012`$~(R->T)->U . ~~U  .: ~~(R->T)`=One too many negations in the second premise.`&
Recog 1.013`$T . T->~Q  .: ~Q`=Note that the order in which the premises appear does not matter.`&

Recog 1.014`$~~~P->Q  .: ~P->Q`=If we restore the dropped parentheses, we will see that the premise is \l"(~~~P->Q)"\l, not \l"~~~(P->Q)"\l, and thus a conditional, not a negation.  Perhaps this is an attempt to apply the rule of DN to just the antecedent of the conditional, the \l"~~~P"\l part.  But rules may never be applied to the interior of a formula.  (Only when the derived rule of Interchange of Equivalents is established will any rules become applicable to the interior of formulas.)`&

Recog 1.016`$P->Y  .: P->Y`=One may wonder about the utility of the rule R.  Its most common use is to bring a line required for boxing and canceling down below the Show line that is to be canceled.  In theory, this rule is dispensable, in the sense that any derivation that uses it can be transformed into a derivation that does not use it.`&
Recog 1.017`$(P->Q)->~~S  .: (P->Q)->S`=This failed attempt to apply DN violates the Prime Directive:  Rules may never be applied to the interior of a formula.`&

Recog 1.018`$~W . W->X  .: ~X`=Another cock-eyed attempt at MT.  Like 1.011, except for the (irrelevant) order of the premises.  If the first premise and the conclusion traded places, it would be a correct application of MT.`&
Recog 1.019`$R->Q  .: ~~R->Q`=Compare 1.014.  The premise, in official notation, is \l"(R->Q)"\l; the conclusion is \l"(~~R->Q)"\l.  This is not a correct application of DN.`&

Recog 1.020`$(P->T)->(R->(S->P)) . (P->T) . R  .: S->P`=The conclusion can be obtained by two applications of MP, the first to premises 1 and 2, the second to the result and premise 3, but it cannot be obtained by a single application of MP.  Using queuing, a correct justification for the conclusion would read, "PR1 PR2 MP PR3 MP".`&
#-The primitive rules for this chapter are:
#-S, Adj, MTP, ADD, BC, and CB.

Recog 2.001`$~(P&Q)  .: ~Q`=This appears to be another attempt to apply an inference rule, here, Simplification, to the interior of a formula (see explanations of answers to problems 1.014 and 1.017 of Chapter I).\nRULES MAY NEVER BE APPLIED TO THE INTERIOR OF A FORMULA.\n(Only when the derived rule of Interchange of Equivalents is established will any rules become applicable to the interior of formulas.)`&
Recog 2.002`$~(P|Q)&((R->~P)<->S)  .: ~(P|Q)`=In Command Mode, one can avoid a query by directly citing the form of the rule, here, Simplification on the left, or SL.`&
Recog 2.003`$~P&Q->R  .: ~P`=The attempt to Simplify reflect an incorrect parsing of the premise, which is correctly parsed as a conditional \l"((~P&Q)->R)"\l not a conjunction.`&

Recog 2.004`$~S|R . P->Q  .: (P->Q)&(~S|R)`=Note that both pairs of parentheses are required in the conclusion; the first by the fact that \l"->"\l is a major connective, the second by the fact that \l"&"\l and \l"|"\l are both minor connectives.`&

Recog 2.006`$(R|S) . Q<->P  .: (R|S)&Q<->P`=This attempt to apply ADJ fails because the conclusion is a biconditional (the major connective as between \l"&"\l and \l"<->"\l).  If the conclusion had been written \l"(R|S)&(Q<->P)"\l, it would have been a correct application of ADJ.`&
Recog 2.007`$~P . ~(Q<->R)  .: ~(P&(Q<->R))`=Perhaps the perpetrator of this argument thought to hold the negations in abeyance while adjoining the negated formulas, then carry down the negation.`&

Recog 2.008`$P->Q  .: P->Q|R`=Like 1.006, this attempt at Addition miscarries because of the lack of parentheses in the conclusion.  A correct application of ADD (more precisely ADDR) would yield \l"(P->Q)|R"\l.`&

Recog 2.009`$R&S  .: Q|(R&S)`=For this correct application of Addition on the Left using the parameter "Q" for the formula to be added, one could simply enter "PR1 ADDL/Q".  In Command Mode, no queries would result.`&

Recog 2.010`$R->S  .: (R->S)|(S->Q)`=As in 2.009, a Command Mode command of \l"PR1 ADDR/(S->Q)"\l would generate the line without queries.  Note that when using parameters, even \l "PR1 ADDR/S->Q"\l will generate the correct line.`&

Recog 2.011`$P&~Q  .: (P|Q)&(~Q|R)`=This doesn't begin to be derivable by the application of a single primitive rule.  However, the following single command, queued and with parameters, will generate the line: "PR1 SL ADDR/Q PR1 SR ADDR/R ADJ".`&
Recog 2.012`$P|Q  .: P|Q|R`=Note that the conclusion is associated to the left.  Thus, in official notation, \l"((P|Q)|R)"\l.`&

Recog 2.013`$P|Q  .: R|P|Q`=As in 2.012, our conventions for dropping parentheses allows them to be dropped for a series of disjuncts only if the disjuncts are associated to the left.  Hence, the conclusion, in official notation, is \l"((R|P)|Q)"\l.  This formula is not directly derivable from \l"(P|Q)"\l by Addition.  Only \l"(R|(P|Q))"\l follows directly by ADD.  In order to get the conclusion as it appears, one must then use the Derived Rule of Assoc (or derive the appropriate instance of T54).`&
Recog 2.015`$P|~(Q&R) . ~P  .:Q&R`=What happened to the negation? This failed attempt at MTP should have had as its conclusion \l"~(Q&R)"\l.`&
Recog 2.016`$P|~(S->(T|R)) . ~P  .: ~(S->(T|R))`=Note that MTP applies equally to either the left disjunct or the right disjunct (compare 2.014).`&
Recog 2.017`$(P|Q)->R . ~P  .: Q`=One can't just ignore the \l"->R"\l.`&
Recog 2.018`$~(P<->Q)  .: ~(P->Q)`=Shame shame! Again, an attempt to apply BC to the interior of a formula (see 2.001).`&

Recog 2.019`$P|~R<->Q&~S  .: Q&~S->P|~R`=Bingo!  This is a correct application of BC in the Right to Left direction.  Either "PR1 BC", which will generate a query about which direction is desired, or "PR1 BCR", which will not generate a query, can be used as justification.`&
Recog 2.020`$P<->Q&R  .: Q->P`=That old devil parsing has blinded the perpetrator.  The premise is indeed a biconditional, \l"(P<->(Q&R))"\l, but the BCR would yield \l"Q&R->P"\l, not \l"Q->P"\l.`&
Recog 2.021`$P&Q->R . R->P&Q  .: R<->P&Q`=The biconditional in either direction can be derived from these two premises.`&

Recog 2.022`$(P->Q)->R . R->(Q->P)  .: R<->(P<->Q)`=This is a sly one.  The \l"(P->Q)"\l gets reversed in the second premise.  The second premise needed to be \l"R->(P->Q)"\l to validly yield any conclusion by CB, and even then it wouldn't yield this conclusion.  (What would it yield?)`&
#-The primitive rules for this chapter are:
#-S, Adj, MTP, ADD, BC, and CB, plus
Recog 3.001`$@x(Fx->Gy)  .: Fx->Gy`=The instantial term is the variable "x" itself.  In the conclusion, the outermost parentheses were dropped in accordance with the conventions.`&
Recog 3.002`$!xFx  .: Fa`=EI, but only on the assumption that that the external constraint is satisfied, namely that the instantial variable "a" has no prior occurrence anywhere in the derivation.`&
Recog 3.003`$Gx  .: @xGx`=There is no inference rule, UG, for universally generalizing a formula.  Instead, we have Universal Derivation (UD) as a new form for boxing & canceling.`&
Recog 3.004`$!yGy  .: GA`=In EI, the instantial term must be a variable; "A" is a name letter, not a variable.`&

Recog 3.005`$@xGy  .: Gy`=The quantifier phrase is vacuous; it binds nothing.  You may wonder what the instantial term is.  Let it be any term, say "A". If we replace all the occurrences of "x" that are bound by the vacuous quantifier, then since there are no such occurrences, we change nothing.`&
Recog 3.006`$!xGy  .: Gz`=As in 3.005, the quantifier phrase is vacuous.  Therefore any application of EI would yield "Gy", not "Gz".`&

Recog 3.008`$!x@y(Fy->Gx)  .: @y(Fy->Gb)`=EI, but only on the assumption that that the external constraint is satisfied, namely that the instantial variable "b" has no prior occurrence anywhere in the derivation.`&

Recog 3.009`$FA->GA  .: !y(FA->Gy)`=The instantial term is "A".  Only the second occurrence was generalized on.  In the premise, the outermost parentheses were dropped, but they were restored, as is required, in the conclusion.`&

Recog 3.010`$!xGy  .: Gy`=The quantifier phrase is vacuous; so we may assume that the instantial variable is the first variable not occurring in the derivation.  It is always correct to EI or UI vacuous quantifier phrases.`&

Recog 3.011`$FA->GA  .: !y(Fy->Gy)`=As in 3.009, the instantial term is "A".  Here all occurrences were generalized on.  In the premise, the outermost parentheses were dropped, but they were restored, as is required, in the conclusion.`&
Recog 3.012`$~@x!y(Fz<->Gy)  .: !z~!y(Fz<->Gy)`=This appears to be an attempt to apply QN, but the rewriting of the variable "x" to "z" prevents this from being a correct application of QN.`&

Recog 3.013`$@x!y(Fx->Gy)  .: !y(Fy->Gy)`=This appears to be an attempt to apply UI, with "y" as the instantial term.  But the occurrence of "y" in "Fy" got picked up by the preexisting quantifier phrase \l"!y"\l.  To put it in more formal terms, not all occurrences of "x" that were bound by the initial universal quantifier were replaced by free occurrences of "y".`&

Recog 3.014`$@x(!z(Fx&Gy)->!xHx|Gx)  .: !z(FA&Gy)->!xHx|Gx`=This appears to be an attempt to apply UI, with "A" as the instantial term, but the final occurrence of "x", which is bound by the relevant universal quantifier, was not replaced.`&

Recog 3.015`$!x(Fx&Gy)  .: Fa&Gy`=EI, but only on the assumption that that the external constraint is satisfied, namely that the instantial variable "a" has no prior occurrence anywhere in the derivation.`&

Recog 3.016`$FA&!x(Gx|GA)  .: !x(Fx&!x(Gx|Gx))`=This appears to be an attempt to apply EG to both occurrences of "A" (as the instantial term), and with "x" as the generalized variable, but the final occurrence of "x" in the conclusion got picked up by the preexisting internal quantifier phrase \l"!x"\l.`&
Recog 3.017`$FA&!x(Gx|GA)  .: !y(Fy&!x(Gx|Gy))`=Compare 3.016.  EG is applied to both occurrences of "A" (as the instantial term), and with "y" as the generalized variable.`&

Recog 3.018`$(@xFx->!y(Hy|Hx))  .: FB->!y(Hy|HB)`=This appears to be an attempt to apply UI, with "B" as the instantial term, but the quantifier phrase \l"@x"\l is not the main connective in the premise, the conditional is, so UI is not applicable. In addition, the universal quantifier phrase does not even bind the final occurrence of "x", which was replaced by "B".`&

Recog 3.019`$@x(Fx->!y(FB&Gy))  .: !z(@xFx->!y(Fz&Gy))`=If the first left parenthesis in the premise had been to the left of the initial quantifier, this would have been a correct application of EG, with "B" as the instantial term and "z" as the generalized variable, but as it is, it is nothing.`&

Recog 3.020`$!z(FA&Gz)->!xHx|GA  .:  !x(!z(FA&Gz)->!xHx|Gx)`=Only the second occurrence of "A" (as the instantial term) is generalized on, and with "x" as the generalized variable.  Note that the final occurrence of "x" in the conclusion is bound by the initial quantifier phrase since it (the final "x") does not lie within the scope of the inner existential quantifier on "x".`&
Recog 3.021`$!z(FA&Gy)->!xHx|GA  .: !x(!z(Fx&Gy)->!xHx|Gx)`=Exactly like 3.020 except that both occurrences of "A" were generalized on.`&
Recog 3.022`$~~!xFx  .: ~@x~Fx`=This appears to be an attempt to apply QN to the interior of a formula, which is never correct.`&
Recog 3.023`$~!x~GA  .: @xGA`=This is one of the less used forms (QN6, in fact). Also, as it happens, the quantifier phrase is vacuous.`&

Recog 3.024`$~@x(Fx|Gx)  .: !x(~Fx&~Gx)`=This is a valid argument, but it cannot be achieved in a single step.  The argument, as given, appears to be a combination of first applying QN to the premise, and then applying one of the DeMorgan laws to the interior of the result.`&
Recog 3.025`$~!x~GA  .: @x~~GA`=Compare 3.023.  This uses a more familiar form of QN (QN3) than 3.023 does.`&
Recog 3.026`$@x@y(Fx&Gy<->Gy&Fx)  .: Fx&Gy<->Gy&Fx`=None, although the result can be achieved by a sequence of two applications of UI, perhaps even queued on a single line.`&

Recog 3.028`$!xFx->FA|@xGx  .: !x(!xFx->Fx|@xGx)`="A" is the instantial term, and "x" is the generalized variable.  Note that the initial existential generalization in the conclusion does not bind any occurrence of "x" except the one that replaces "A".`&
Recog 3.029`$!y@x(Fx|Gx)  .: @y!x(~Fx&~Gx)`=The conclusion, in fact, is equivalent to the negation of the premise; it certainly is not a consequence of it.`&

Recog 3.030`$@x(Fx->!y(FB&Gy))  .: @x(Fx->!z!y(Fz&Gy))`=This appears to be an attempt to apply EG to the interior of a formula, in fact, to just the consequent of the inner conditional (with "B" as the instantial term, and "z" as the generalized variable).`&

Recog 3.031`$@x(!zFz->@zGz|Fx)  .: @z(!zFz->@zGz|Fz)`=The generalized variable "x" in the premise is rewritten to "z".  Note that the preexisting occurrences of "z" continue to be bound to the same occurrences of quantifiers.`&

Recog 3.032`$@x(!xFx->@z(Gz|Fx))  .: @z(!xFx->@z(Gz|Fz))`=This appears to be an attempt to apply AV by rewriting the generalized variable "x" in the premise to "z".  But the final occurrence of a variable ("x" in the premise, "z" in the conclusion) is no longer bound to the initial quantifier phrase.`&

Recog 3.033`$!x(Fz<->@zGz|Fx)  .: !z(Fz<->@zGz|Fz)`=This also appears to be an attempt to apply AV by rewriting the generalized variable "x" in the premise to "z".  But this time the first occurrence of the variable "z", which is free in the premise, gets picked up by the rewritten initial quantifier phrase.`&
#-The primitive rules for this chapter are:
#-S, Adj, MTP, ADD, BC, and CB, plus
Recog 4.001`$@x!zF(A(xyx)z)  .: !zF(zz)`=This looks like an attempt to use UI, but there is no way to replace "x" in "A(xyx)" and come out with just "z".`&
Recog 4.004`$@x!zF(A(xyx)z)  .: !zF(A(xxx)z)`=This looks like an attempt to use UI, but replacing the bound variable "x" by "x" would yield "A(xyx)" not "A(xxx)".`&
Recog 4.005`$@x!zF(A(xyx)z)  .: !zF(A(CyB)z)`=This looks like an attempt to use UI, but both "B" and "C" have been used to replace "x".  You cannot UI to two different terms at once.`&

Recog 4.010`$@x!zF(A(xyx)z)  .: !zF(A(B(C(z))yB(C(z)))z)`=This looks like an attempt to use UI, but when the bound variable "x" is replaced by "B(C(z))", the free "z" in "B(C(z))" is captured by the "\l!z\l" quantifier.`&

Recog 4.013`$@xFA(xB(y))|G(Cy)  .: !w(@xFw|G(Cy))`=This looks like an attempt to use EG by generalizing on the term "A(xB(y))", but this term is bound in the original formula because it contains a bound occurrence of a variable (the "x" is bound by the universal quantifier).  You cannot existentially generalize on a bound term.`&
Recog 4.016`$@xFA(xB(y))|G(Cy)  .: !x(@xFA(xB(y))|G(xy))`=Congratulations!  Note that the new initial quantifier, "\l!x\l", does not bind anything in the left disjunct.`&

Recog 4.017`$@xFA(xB(y))|G(Cy)  .: !x(@xFA(xB(x))|G(Cx))`=This looks like an attempt to use EG by generalizing on the free "y"s, but note that when the first "y" is replaced by "x", the new occurrence of "x" gets captured by the wrong quantifier.  It is bound by the original universal quantifier rather than the newly introduced existential quantifier.  The new occurrences of the variable introduced by an EG must all be bound to the new existential quantifier.  `&
Recog 4.019`$@xFA(xB(y))|G(Cy)  .: !y(@xFA(xB(y))|G(yy))`=This looks like an attempt to use EG on "C", but in the course of it, the two free occurrences of "y" have been picked up. `&
Recog 4.020`$@xFA(xB(y))|G(Cy)  .: !x(@xFA(xB(y))|G(Cy))`="\l!x\l" does not bind anything, but that is okay.  It is a "vacuous" quantifier.`&

Recog 4.021`$@xFA(xB(y))|G(Cy)  .: !w(@xFA(xB(y))|Gw)`=This looks like an attempt to use EG, but "G(Cy)" cannot be obtained from "Gw" by proper substitution.  In the former, "G" is a two-place predicate; in the latter it is monadic. `&
#-The primitive rules for this chapter add:
#-S, Adj, MTP, ADD, BC, and CB, plus
Recog 5.001`$~!zG(xzx) . !zG(yzx) .: x <> y`=LL.LL3`@This is a correct application of LL, in particular of LL3.`&
Recog 5.002`$A(x)=B(y) .: B(y)=A(x)`=SM.SM1`@This is a correct application of SM, in particular of SM1.`&

Recog 5.003`$!zG(xzx) . y=x .: !zG(yzy)`=LL.LL2`@This is a correct application of LL, in particular of LL2.  In Command Mode, there would be a query as to which of the (free) occurrences of "x" you wish to replace by "y".  The answer here was "both of them".`&
Recog 5.004`$A(x)<>B(y) .: B(y)<>A(x)`=SM.SM2`@This is a correct application of SM, in particular of SM2.`&

Recog 5.005`$!xF(xy) . y=x .: !xF(xx)`=none`@This looks like an attempt to use LL to replace the free "y" by "x", but the fact that the replacement gets captured by the quantifier makes it incorrect.`&

Recog 5.006`$A(x)=B(y) .: A(A(x))=A(B(y))`=EL`@This is a correct application of EL.  The fact that the identity in the premise is between already complex terms only means that you must examine the conclusion more carefully.`&

Recog 5.007`$!xF(xy) . x=y .: !xF(yy)`=none`@Like 5.005, this looks like an attempt to use LL to replace "x" by "y", but here the occurrence of the term being replaced, "x", was not free.  This makes the replacement incorrect.`&

Recog 5.008`$A(x)<>B(x) .: C(A(x))<>C(B(x))`=none`@This looks like an attempt to use EL.  But EL doesn't occur in the form "~D=E .: ~C(D)=C(E)", and would not be valid if it did.  Remember that although ~2=-2 (two is not negative two) the square of 2 is the same number as the square of -2.`&
Recog 5.009`$!zF(zB(A(x))) . ~!zF(zB(B(y))) .: A(x)<>B(y)`=LL.LL4`@This is a correct, though complex, application of LL, in particular of LL4.`&

Recog 5.010`$!xA(x)=B(x) .: C(A(x)) = C(B(x))`=none`@This looks like an attempt to use EL.  But EL doesn't allow its premise to occur only as a subformula of another formula.  From the given premise, you could EI to "A(a)=B(a)", and then you could legitimately apply EL to obtain "C(A(a)) = C(B(a))".`&

Recog 5.011`$!yF(yB(A(x))) . A(x)=B(y) .: !yF(yB(B(y)))`=none`@Like 5.005, this looks like an attempt to use LL to replace the free "A(x)" by "B(y)", but the fact that this replacement also gets captured by the quantifier makes the inference incorrect.  Remember, a term is bound if it contains a bound occurrence of any variable.`&

Recog 5.012`$A(x)=B(x) .: C(A(x)B(x))=C(B(x)B(x))`=EL`@This is a correct application of EL.  Here the complex term into which the replacement is being made is "C( __ B(x))", with "C" a 2-place operation symbol, and "B" a 1-place operation symbol.  If you prove T305 to derive EL from LL and SID, you may see more clearly why EL, like LL1, allows you to replace any number of the (free) occurrences of the premise's left-hand term by (free) occurrences of the premise's right-hand term.`&

lines: #  problem:                 problem name, as shown in the problem list
#  options:                 per-problem options, e.g. eg (a worked example)
#  note:                    note shown under the problem title
#  common-name:             common name of the problem (course database)
#  original-name:           name the problem was copied from
#  seconds:                 time worked, in seconds (saved work)
#  notation:                chosen notation: O official, I informal, N not well formed
#  expansion:               which parse-tree nodes are expanded
#  problem:                 problem name, as shown in the problem list
#  options:                 per-problem options, e.g. eg (a worked example)
#  note:                    note shown under the problem title
#  common-name:             common name of the problem (course database)
#  original-name:           name the problem was copied from
#  seconds:                 time worked, in seconds (saved work)
#  correct-rules:           rules that are accepted as correct answers, separated by '.'
#  near-miss-rules:         rules that get a 'nearly right' response
#  comment:                 comment shown after a correct answer
#-The primitive rules of this chapter are:

Recog 1.001`$P->P . P  .: P`=This is a perfectly correct application of MP.  The fact that the rule is stated using distinct antecedent and consequent allows the antecedent and consequent to be distinct, but does not require it.`&Recog 1.001`C
Recog 1.002`$~T->(T->U) . ~(T->U)  .: ~~T`=Note that the conclusion must be as given, and cannot be "T", which is not the negation of the antecedent of the conditional.`&Recog 1.002`C

Recog 1.004`$~(~P->W)  .: P->W`=The premise is the negation of a conditional, not the negation of a negation.  If the premise had been \l"~~(P->W)"\l the conclusion could have been obtained by DN.`&Recog 1.004`C

Recog 1.005`$~Q->~R . R  .: Q`=The second premise is not the negation of the consequent of the conditional (as is required), and the conclusion is not the negation of the antecedent of the conditional (as is also required).  The result can be obtained from those two premises, but not directly by a single application of MT.  Rather, one must first apply DN to the second premise, then apply MT to obtain \l"~~Q"\l, then apply a second DN to that result.`&Recog 1.005`C
Recog 1.007`$(~Q->S)->P . ~Q->S  .: P`=Note that the "official" outermost parentheses have been dropped in the second premise, but cannot be dropped in the first premise.`&Recog 1.007`C

Recog 1.009`$~~P->~Q . ~~Q  .: ~P`=This case is rather like 1.005.  Although MT can be applied directly to these premises, it yields \l"~~~P"\l rather than \l"~P"\l.  The latter requires an application of DN.`&Recog 1.009`C
Recog 1.010`$T->S  .: ~~(T->S)`=As in 1.007, the "official" outermost parentheses have been dropped in the premise, but cannot be dropped in the conclusion.`&Recog 1.010`C

Recog 1.011`$P->Y . ~P  .: ~Y`=A wrong way around attempt to apply MT.  To apply MT, the second premise must be the negation of the consequent of the conditional rather than being the negation of the antecedent.`&Recog 1.011`C
Recog 1.012`$~(R->T)->U . ~~U  .: ~~(R->T)`=One too many negations in the second premise.`&Recog 1.012`C
Recog 1.013`$T . T->~Q  .: ~Q`=Note that the order in which the premises appear does not matter.`&Recog 1.013`C

Recog 1.014`$~~~P->Q  .: ~P->Q`=If we restore the dropped parentheses, we will see that the premise is \l"(~~~P->Q)"\l, not \l"~~~(P->Q)"\l, and thus a conditional, not a negation.  Perhaps this is an attempt to apply the rule of DN to just the antecedent of the conditional, the \l"~~~P"\l part.  But rules may never be applied to the interior of a formula.  (Only when the derived rule of Interchange of Equivalents is established will any rules become applicable to the interior of formulas.)`&Recog 1.014`C

Recog 1.016`$P->Y  .: P->Y`=One may wonder about the utility of the rule R.  Its most common use is to bring a line required for boxing and canceling down below the Show line that is to be canceled.  In theory, this rule is dispensable, in the sense that any derivation that uses it can be transformed into a derivation that does not use it.`&Recog 1.016`C
Recog 1.017`$(P->Q)->~~S  .: (P->Q)->S`=This failed attempt to apply DN violates the Prime Directive:  Rules may never be applied to the interior of a formula.`&Recog 1.017`C

Recog 1.018`$~W . W->X  .: ~X`=Another cock-eyed attempt at MT.  Like 1.011, except for the (irrelevant) order of the premises.  If the first premise and the conclusion traded places, it would be a correct application of MT.`&Recog 1.018`C
Recog 1.019`$R->Q  .: ~~R->Q`=Compare 1.014.  The premise, in official notation, is \l"(R->Q)"\l; the conclusion is \l"(~~R->Q)"\l.  This is not a correct application of DN.`&Recog 1.019`C

Recog 1.020`$(P->T)->(R->(S->P)) . (P->T) . R  .: S->P`=The conclusion can be obtained by two applications of MP, the first to premises 1 and 2, the second to the result and premise 3, but it cannot be obtained by a single application of MP.  Using queuing, a correct justification for the conclusion would read, "PR1 PR2 MP PR3 MP".`&Recog 1.020`C
#-The primitive rules for this chapter are:
#-S, Adj, MTP, ADD, BC, and CB.

Recog 2.001`$~(P&Q)  .: ~Q`=This appears to be another attempt to apply an inference rule, here, Simplification, to the interior of a formula (see explanations of answers to problems 1.014 and 1.017 of Chapter I).\nRULES MAY NEVER BE APPLIED TO THE INTERIOR OF A FORMULA.\n(Only when the derived rule of Interchange of Equivalents is established will any rules become applicable to the interior of formulas.)`&Recog 2.001`C
Recog 2.002`$~(P|Q)&((R->~P)<->S)  .: ~(P|Q)`=In Command Mode, one can avoid a query by directly citing the form of the rule, here, Simplification on the left, or SL.`&Recog 2.002`C
Recog 2.003`$~P&Q->R  .: ~P`=The attempt to Simplify reflect an incorrect parsing of the premise, which is correctly parsed as a conditional \l"((~P&Q)->R)"\l not a conjunction.`&Recog 2.003`C

Recog 2.004`$~S|R . P->Q  .: (P->Q)&(~S|R)`=Note that both pairs of parentheses are required in the conclusion; the first by the fact that \l"->"\l is a major connective, the second by the fact that \l"&"\l and \l"|"\l are both minor connectives.`&Recog 2.004`C

Recog 2.006`$(R|S) . Q<->P  .: (R|S)&Q<->P`=This attempt to apply ADJ fails because the conclusion is a biconditional (the major connective as between \l"&"\l and \l"<->"\l).  If the conclusion had been written \l"(R|S)&(Q<->P)"\l, it would have been a correct application of ADJ.`&Recog 2.006`C

Recog 2.007`$~P . ~(Q<->R)  .: ~(P&(Q<->R))`=Perhaps the perpetrator of this argument thought to hold the negations in abeyance while adjoining the negated formulas, then carry down the negation.`&Recog 2.007`C

Recog 2.008`$P->Q  .: P->Q|R`=Like 1.006, this attempt at Addition miscarries because of the lack of parentheses in the conclusion.  A correct application of ADD (more precisely ADDR) would yield \l"(P->Q)|R"\l.`&Recog 2.008`C

Recog 2.009`$R&S  .: Q|(R&S)`=For this correct application of Addition on the Left using the parameter "Q" for the formula to be added, one could simply enter "PR1 ADDL/Q".  In Command Mode, no queries would result.`&Recog 2.009`C

Recog 2.010`$R->S  .: (R->S)|(S->Q)`=As in 2.009, a Command Mode command of \l"PR1 ADDR/(S->Q)"\l would generate the line without queries.  Note that when using parameters, even \l "PR1 ADDR/S->Q"\l will generate the correct line.`&Recog 2.010`C

Recog 2.011`$P&~Q  .: (P|Q)&(~Q|R)`=This doesn't begin to be derivable by the application of a single primitive rule.  However, the following single command, queued and with parameters, will generate the line: "PR1 SL ADDR/Q PR1 SR ADDR/R ADJ".`&Recog 2.011`C
Recog 2.012`$P|Q  .: P|Q|R`=Note that the conclusion is associated to the left.  Thus, in official notation, \l"((P|Q)|R)"\l.`&Recog 2.012`C

Recog 2.013`$P|Q  .: R|P|Q`=As in 2.012, our conventions for dropping parentheses allows them to be dropped for a series of disjuncts only if the disjuncts are associated to the left.  Hence, the conclusion, in official notation, is \l"((R|P)|Q)"\l.  This formula is not directly derivable from \l"(P|Q)"\l by Addition.  Only \l"(R|(P|Q))"\l follows directly by ADD.  In order to get the conclusion as it appears, one must then use the Derived Rule of Assoc (or derive the appropriate instance of T54).`&Recog 2.013`C
Recog 2.015`$P|~(Q&R) . ~P  .:Q&R`=What happened to the negation? This failed attempt at MTP should have had as its conclusion \l"~(Q&R)"\l.`&Recog 2.015`C
Recog 2.016`$P|~(S->(T|R)) . ~P  .: ~(S->(T|R))`=Note that MTP applies equally to either the left disjunct or the right disjunct (compare 2.014).`&Recog 2.016`C
Recog 2.017`$(P|Q)->R . ~P  .: Q`=One can't just ignore the \l"->R"\l.`&Recog 2.017`C
Recog 2.018`$~(P<->Q)  .: ~(P->Q)`=Shame shame! Again, an attempt to apply BC to the interior of a formula (see 2.001).`&Recog 2.018`C

Recog 2.019`$P|~R<->Q&~S  .: Q&~S->P|~R`=Bingo!  This is a correct application of BC in the Right to Left direction.  Either "PR1 BC", which will generate a query about which direction is desired, or "PR1 BCR", which will not generate a query, can be used as justification.`&Recog 2.019`C

Recog 2.020`$P<->Q&R  .: Q->P`=That old devil parsing has blinded the perpetrator.  The premise is indeed a biconditional, \l"(P<->(Q&R))"\l, but the BCR would yield \l"Q&R->P"\l, not \l"Q->P"\l.`&Recog 2.020`C
Recog 2.021`$P&Q->R . R->P&Q  .: R<->P&Q`=The biconditional in either direction can be derived from these two premises.`&Recog 2.021`C

Recog 2.022`$(P->Q)->R . R->(Q->P)  .: R<->(P<->Q)`=This is a sly one.  The \l"(P->Q)"\l gets reversed in the second premise.  The second premise needed to be \l"R->(P->Q)"\l to validly yield any conclusion by CB, and even then it wouldn't yield this conclusion.  (What would it yield?)`&Recog 2.022`C
#-The primitive rules for this chapter are:
#-S, Adj, MTP, ADD, BC, and CB, plus
Recog 3.001`$@x(Fx->Gy)  .: Fx->Gy`=The instantial term is the variable "x" itself.  In the conclusion, the outermost parentheses were dropped in accordance with the conventions.`&Recog 3.001`C

Recog 3.002`$!xFx  .: Fi`=EI, but only on the assumption that that the external constraint is satisfied, namely that the instantial variable "i" has no prior occurrence anywhere in the derivation.`&Recog 3.002`C
Recog 3.003`$Gx  .: @xGx`=There is no inference rule, UG, for universally generalizing a formula.  Instead, we have Universal Derivation (UD) as a new form for boxing & canceling.`&Recog 3.003`C
Recog 3.004`$!yGy  .: Ga`=In EI, the instantial term must be a variable; "a" is a name letter, not a variable.`&Recog 3.004`C

Recog 3.005`$@xGy  .: Gy`=The quantifier phrase is vacuous; it binds nothing.  You may wonder what the instantial term is.  Let it be any term, say "a". If we replace all the occurrences of "x" that are bound by the vacuous quantifier, then since there are no such occurrences, we change nothing.`&Recog 3.005`C
Recog 3.006`$!xGy  .: Gi`=As in 3.005, the quantifier phrase is vacuous.  Therefore any application of EI would yield "Gy", not "Gi".`&Recog 3.006`C

Recog 3.008`$!x@y(Fy->Gx)  .: @y(Fy->Gj)`=EI, but only on the assumption that that the external constraint is satisfied, namely that the instantial variable "j" has no prior occurrence anywhere in the derivation.`&Recog 3.008`C

Recog 3.009`$Fa->Ga  .: !y(Fa->Gy)`=The instantial term is "a".  Only the second occurrence was generalized on.  In the premise, the outermost parentheses were dropped, but they were restored, as is required, in the conclusion.`&Recog 3.009`C

Recog 3.010`$!xGy  .: Gy`=The quantifier phrase is vacuous; so we may assume that the instantial variable is the first variable not occurring in the derivation.  It is always correct to EI or UI vacuous quantifier phrases.`&Recog 3.010`C

Recog 3.011`$Fa->Ga  .: !y(Fy->Gy)`=As in 3.009, the instantial term is "a".  Here all occurrences were generalized on.  In the premise, the outermost parentheses were dropped, but they were restored, as is required, in the conclusion.`&Recog 3.011`C

Recog 3.012`$~@x!y(Fz<->Gy)  .: !z~!y(Fz<->Gy)`=This appears to be an attempt to apply QN, but the rewriting of the variable "x" to "z" prevents this from being a correct application of QN.`&Recog 3.012`C

Recog 3.013`$@x!y(Fx->Gy)  .: !y(Fy->Gy)`=This appears to be an attempt to apply UI, with "y" as the instantial term.  but the occurrence of "y" in "Fy" got picked up by the preexisting quantifier phrase \l"!y"\l.  To put it in more formal terms, not all occurrences of "x" that were bound by the initial universal quantifier were replaced by free occurrences of "y".`&Recog 3.013`C

Recog 3.014`$@x(!z(Fx&Gy)->!xHx|Gx)  .: !z(Fa&Gy)->!xHx|Gx`=This appears to be an attempt to apply UI, with "a" as the instantial term, but the final occurrence of "x", which is bound by the relevant universal quantifier, was not replaced.`&Recog 3.014`C

Recog 3.015`$!x(Fx&Gy)  .: Fi&Gy`=EI, but only on the assumption that that the external constraint is satisfied, namely that the instantial variable "i" has no prior occurrence anywhere in the derivation.`&Recog 3.015`C

Recog 3.016`$Fa&!x(Gx|Ga)  .: !x(Fx&!x(Gx|Gx))`=This appears to be an attempt to apply EG to both occurrences of "a" (as the instantial term), and with "x" as the generalized variable, but the final occurrence of "x" in the conclusion got picked up by the preexisting internal quantifier phrase \l"!x"\l.`&Recog 3.016`C
Recog 3.017`$Fa&!x(Gx|Ga)  .: !y(Fy&!x(Gx|Gy))`=Compare 3.016.  EG is applied to both occurrences of "a" (as the instantial term), and with "y" as the generalized variable.`&Recog 3.017`C

Recog 3.018`$(@xFx->!y(Hy|Hx))  .: Fb->!y(Hy|Hb)`=This appears to be an attempt to apply UI, with "b" as the instantial term, but the quantifier phrase \l"@x"\l is not the main connective in the premise, the conditional is, so UI is not applicable. In addition, the universal quantifier phrase does not even bind the final occurrence of "x", which was replaced by "b".`&Recog 3.018`C

Recog 3.019`$@x(Fx->!y(Fb&Gy))  .: !z(@xFx->!y(Fz&Gy))`=If the first left parenthesis in the premise had been to the left of the initial quantifier, this would have been a correct application of EG, with "b" as the instantial term and "z" as the generalized variable, but as it is, it is nothing.`&Recog 3.019`C

Recog 3.020`$!z(Fa&Gz)->!xHx|Ga  .:  !x(!z(Fa&Gz)->!xHx|Gx)`=Only the second occurrence of "a" (as the instantial term) is generalized on, and with "x" as the generalized variable.  Note that the final occurrence of "x" in the conclusion is bound by the initial quantifier phrase since it (the final "x") does not lie within the scope of the inner existential quantifier on "x".`&Recog 3.020`C
Recog 3.021`$!z(Fa&Gy)->!xHx|Ga  .: !x(!z(Fx&Gy)->!xHx|Gx)`=Exactly like 3.020 except that both occurrences of "a" were generalized on.`&Recog 3.021`C
Recog 3.022`$~~!xFx  .: ~@x~Fx`=This appears to be an attempt to apply QN to the interior of a formula, which is never correct.`&Recog 3.022`C
Recog 3.023`$~!x~Ga  .: @xGa`=This is one of the less used forms (QN6, in fact). Also, as it happens, the quantifier phrase is vacuous.`&Recog 3.023`C

Recog 3.024`$~@x(Fx|Gx)  .: !x(~Fx&~Gx)`=This is a valid argument, but it cannot be achieved in a single step.  The argument, as given, appears to be a combination of first applying QN to the premise, and then applying one of the DeMorgan laws to the interior of the result.`&Recog 3.024`C
Recog 3.025`$~!x~Ga  .: @x~~Ga`=Compare 3.023.  This uses a more familiar form of QN (QN3) than 3.023 does.`&Recog 3.025`C
Recog 3.026`$@x@y(Fx&Gy<->Gy&Fx)  .: Fx&Gy<->Gy&Fx`=None, although the result can be achieved by a sequence of two applications of UI, perhaps even queued on a single line.`&Recog 3.026`C

Recog 3.028`$!xFx->Fa|@xGx  .: !x(!xFx->Fx|@xGx)`="a" is the instantial term, and "x" is the generalized variable.  Note that the initial existential generalization in the conclusion does not bind any occurrence of "x" except the one that replaces "a".`&Recog 3.028`C
Recog 3.029`$!y@x(Fx|Gx)  .: @y!x(~Fx&~Gx)`=The conclusion, in fact, is equivalent to the negation of the premise; it certainly is not a consequence of it.`&Recog 3.029`C

Recog 3.030`$@x(Fx->!y(Fb&Gy))  .: @x(Fx->!z!y(Fz&Gy))`=This appears to be an attempt to apply EG to the interior of a formula, in fact, to just the consequent of the inner conditional (with "b" as the instantial term, and "z" as the generalized variable).`&Recog 3.030`C

Recog 3.031`$@x(!zFz->@zGz|Fx)  .: @z(!zFz->@zGz|Fz)`=The generalized variable "x" in the premise is rewritten to "z".  Note that the preexisting occurrences of "z" continue to be bound to the same occurrences of quantifiers.`&Recog 3.031`C

Recog 3.032`$@x(!xFx->@z(Gz|Fx))  .: @z(!xFx->@z(Gz|Fz))`=This appears to be an attempt to apply AV by rewriting the generalized variable "x" in the premise to "z".  but the final occurrence of a variable ("x" in the premise, "z" in the conclusion) is no longer bound to the initial quantifier phrase.`&Recog 3.032`C

Recog 3.033`$!x(Fz<->@zGz|Fx)  .: !z(Fz<->@zGz|Fz)`=This also appears to be an attempt to apply AV by rewriting the generalized variable "x" in the premise to "z".  But this time the first occurrence of the variable "z", which is free in the premise, gets picked up by the rewritten initial quantifier phrase.`&Recog 3.033`C
#-The primitive rules for this chapter are:
#-S, Adj, MTP, ADD, BC, and CB, plus
Recog 4.001`$@x!zF(a(xyx)z)  .: !zF(zz)`=This looks like an attempt to use UI, but there is no way to replace "x" in "a(xyx)" and come out with just "z".`&Recog 4.001`C
Recog 4.004`$@x!zF(a(xyx)z)  .: !zF(a(xxx)z)`=This looks like an attempt to use UI, but replacing the bound variable "x" by "x" would yield "a(xyx)" not "a(xxx)".`&Recog 4.004`C
Recog 4.005`$@x!zF(a(xyx)z)  .: !zF(a(cyb)z)`=This looks like an attempt to use UI, but both "b" and "c" have been used to replace "x".  You cannot UI to two different terms at once.`&Recog 4.005`C

Recog 4.010`$@x!zF(a(xyx)z)  .: !zF(a(b(c(z))yb(c(z)))z)`=This looks like an attempt to use UI, but when the bound variable "x" is replaced by "b(c(z))", the free "z" in "b(c(z))" is captured by the "\l!z\l" quantifier.`&Recog 4.010`C

Recog 4.013`$@xFa(xb(y))|G(cy)  .: !w(@xFw|G(cy))`=This looks like an attempt to use EG by generalizing on the term "a(xb(y))", but this term is bound in the original formula because it contains a bound occurrence of a variable (the "x" is bound by the universal quantifier).  You cannot existentially generalize on a bound term.`&Recog 4.013`C
Recog 4.016`$@xFa(xb(y))|G(cy)  .: !x(@xFa(xb(y))|G(xy))`=Congratulations!  Note that the new initial quantifier, "\l!x\l", does not bind anything in the left disjunct.`&Recog 4.016`C

Recog 4.017`$@xFa(xb(y))|G(cy)  .: !x(@xFa(xb(x))|G(cx))`=This looks like an attempt to use EG by generalizing on the free "y"s, but note that when the first "y" is replaced by "x", the new occurrence of "x" gets captured by the wrong quantifier.  It is bound by the original universal quantifier rather than the newly introduced existential quantifier.  The new occurrences of the variable introduced by an EG must all be bound to the new existential quantifier.  `&Recog 4.017`C
Recog 4.019`$@xFa(xb(y))|G(cy)  .: !y(@xFa(xb(y))|G(yy))`=This looks like an attempt to use EG on "c", but in the course of it, the two free occurrences of "y" have been picked up. `&Recog 4.019`C
Recog 4.020`$@xFa(xb(y))|G(cy)  .: !x(@xFa(xb(y))|G(cy))`="\l!x\l" does not bind anything, but that is okay.  It is a "vacuous" quantifier.`&Recog 4.020`C

Recog 4.021`$@xFa(xb(y))|G(cy)  .: !w(@xFa(xb(y))|Gw)`=This looks like an attempt to use EG, but "G(cy)" cannot be obtained from "Gw" by proper substitution.  In the former, "G" is a two-place predicate; in the latter it is monadic. `&Recog 4.021`C
#-The primitive rules for this chapter add:
#-S, Adj, MTP, ADD, BC, and CB, plus
Recog 5.001`$~!zG(xzx) . !zG(yzx) .: x <> y`=LL.LL3`@This is a correct application of LL, in particular of LL3.`&Recog 5.001`C
Recog 5.002`$a(x)=b(y) .: b(y)=a(x)`=SM.SM1`@This is a correct application of SM, in particular of SM1.`&Recog 5.002`C

Recog 5.003`$!zG(xzx) . y=x .: !zG(yzy)`=LL.LL2`@This is a correct application of LL, in particular of LL2.  In Command Mode, there would be a query as to which of the (free) occurrences of "x" you wish to replace by "y".  The answer here was "both of them".`&Recog 5.003`C
Recog 5.004`$a(x)<>b(y) .: b(y)<>a(x)`=SM.SM2`@This is a correct application of SM, in particular of SM2.`&Recog 5.004`C

Recog 5.005`$!xF(xy) . y=x .: !xF(xx)`=none`@This looks like an attempt to use LL to replace the free "y" by "x", but the fact that the replacement gets captured by the quantifier makes it incorrect.`&Recog 5.005`C

Recog 5.006`$a(x)=b(y) .: a(a(x))=a(b(y))`=EL`@This is a correct application of EL.  The fact that the identity in the premise is between already complex terms only means that you must examine the conclusion more carefully.`&Recog 5.006`C

Recog 5.007`$!xF(xy) . x=y .: !xF(yy)`=none`@Like 5.005, this looks like an attempt to use LL to replace "x" by "y", but here the occurrence of the term being replaced, "x", was not free.  This makes the replacement incorrect.`&Recog 5.007`C

Recog 5.008`$a(x)<>b(x) .: c(a(x))<>c(b(x))`=none`@This looks like an attempt to use EL.  But EL doesn't occur in the form "~d=e .: ~c(d)=c(e)", and would not be valid if it did.  Remember that although ~2=-2 (two is not negative two) the square of 2 is the same number as the square of -2.`&Recog 5.008`C
Recog 5.009`$!zF(zb(a(x))) . ~!zF(zb(b(y))) .: a(x)<>b(y)`=LL.LL4`@This is a correct, though complex, application of LL, in particular of LL4.`&Recog 5.009`C

Recog 5.010`$!xa(x)=b(x) .: c(a(x)) = c(b(x))`=none`@This looks like an attempt to use EL.  But EL doesn't allow its premise to occur only as a subformula of another formula.  From the given premise, you could EI to "a(i)=b(i)", and then you could legitimately apply EL to obtain "c(a(i)) = c(b(i))".`&Recog 5.010`C

Recog 5.011`$!yF(yb(a(x))) . a(x)=b(y) .: !yF(yb(b(y)))`=none`@Like 5.005, this looks like an attempt to use LL to replace the free "a(x)" by "b(y)", but the fact that this replacement also gets captured by the quantifier makes the inference incorrect.  Remember, a term is bound if it contains a bound occurrence of any variable.`&Recog 5.011`C

Recog 5.012`$a(x)=b(x) .: c(a(x)b(x))=c(b(x)b(x))`=EL`@This is a correct application of EL.  Here the complex term into which the replacement is being made is "c( __ b(x))", with "c" a 2-place operation symbol, and "b" a 1-place operation symbol.  If you prove T305 to derive EL from LL and SID, you may see more clearly why EL, like LL1, allows you to replace any number of the (free) occurrences of the premise's left-hand term by (free) occurrences of the premise's right-hand term.`&Recog 5.012`C

#'## text' lines are headings shown in the program's lists.
